LO.text: Students will be able to define user-defined data types and explain why programmers use them
Students will be able to distinguish between non-composite and composite data types

Activities.text: Starter: 'What You Should Already Know' — students attempt the two warm-up questions (select appropriate primitive data types; write pseudocode for an animal record structure)
Teacher-led explanation of why built-in data types are insufficient for complex programs, introducing user-defined data types with real-world examples
Paired discussion: Activity 13C Q1 and Q2 — explain the difference between composite and non-composite types with examples

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: give one example of a situation where a programmer would need a non-composite user-defined data type and one where they would need a composite type — justify each choice

Homework.text: Read section 13.1 and complete Activity 13C Q3 — choose an appropriate user-defined data type for each scenario and justify your answer in writing

LO.text: Students will be able to define and declare an enumerated data type in pseudocode
Students will be able to declare variables of an enumerated type and assign values to them

Activities.text: Recap quiz: what is the difference between a composite and non-composite data type? (3 questions, cold-call)
Teacher-led worked example: declaring Tmonth enumerated type and variables thisMonth/nextMonth using the textbook pseudocode
Individual task: Activity 13A — declare an enumerated type for days of the week, declare today/yesterday variables, and write suitable assignment statements

Consolidation.text: Students write the pseudocode for a new enumerated type of their own choosing (e.g. seasons, traffic light states, compass directions) and share with a partner to check syntax

Homework.text: Write pseudocode to declare an enumerated type for the suits in a pack of cards. Declare two variables and write assignment statements. Annotate each line to explain what it does

LO.text: Students will be able to define and use a pointer data type in pseudocode
Students will be able to define and use composite data types including sets and records

Activities.text: Teacher-led explanation of pointer data types — using the Tmonth/TmonthPointer example from the textbook, including dereferencing (^ notation)
Individual task: Activity 13B — declare a pointer for the days-of-the-week enumerated type and set it to point at today
Class discussion of composite types: recap records from Chapter 10, then introduce sets (Sletter/vowel example) and briefly introduce classes as composite types

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: what does the ^ symbol mean in a pointer type definition? What is dereferencing? What is the difference between a set and a record?

Homework.text: Complete Activity 13C in full (all three parts). Write pseudocode for a record to store house-for-sale data and an enumerated type for a fixed set of colours — justify your choices

LO.text: Students will be able to describe serial and sequential file organisation methods
Students will be able to compare and contrast serial and sequential files including how records are added

Activities.text: Starter: 'What You Should Already Know' — students attempt the three warm-up questions on file modes and pseudocode file operations (individual, 8 mins)
Teacher-led explanation of serial file organisation using Figure 13.1 — records stored in order of arrival, new records appended, used for transaction files
Teacher-led explanation of sequential file organisation using Figures 13.2 and 13.3 — records sorted by key field, inserting Customer 5 example; class annotates diagrams

Consolidation.text: Students complete a comparison table: serial vs sequential — definition, order of records, how new records are added, a real-world use case for each

Homework.text: Activity 13E Q1 — explain, using examples, the difference between serial and sequential files. Write at least two paragraphs with diagrams

LO.text: Students will be able to describe random file organisation and explain sequential and direct access methods
Students will be able to choose an appropriate file organisation and access method for a given scenario

Activities.text: Recap: quick-fire questions on serial vs sequential files (3 minutes)
Teacher-led explanation of random file organisation using Figure 13.4 — records stored at hashed positions, not in order

Teacher-led comparison of sequential access vs direct access — when each is appropriate (high hit rate vs low hit rate), using the monthly billing and single customer update examples from the textbook
Group task: Activity 13E Q3 — choose the appropriate file type for three scenarios (library, annual tax statement, remote weather station) and justify with reasons

Consolidation.text: Traffic light self-assessment: can students explain the difference between file organisation and file access, and give a use case for each of the three organisation methods?

Homework.text: Write exam-style short answers: (a) explain what is meant by direct access; (b) explain why direct access is preferred when a file has a low hit rate; (c) describe one disadvantage of sequential access

LO.text: Students will be able to explain what a hashing algorithm is and how it is used to store and retrieve records
Students will be able to calculate a file address using a hashing algorithm and explain how collisions are handled

Activities.text: Teacher-led explanation of hashing algorithms using the textbook example: key field 3024, file start 0, 2000 record spaces — calculate address 1024 (Table 13.1); then collision with key 5024 (Table 13.2)
Class works through: what is a collision? Two solutions — open hash (next free space) and closed hash (overflow area)

Individual task: Activity 13D — calculate the address for key field 9354 using the given algorithm (start 500, record size 5, 1000 spaces); then find the next open-hash address if the location is taken

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: describe in your own words how a hashing algorithm is used to store and then retrieve a record using direct access — include what happens if a collision occurs

Homework.text: Activity 13E Q2 — explain the process of direct access to a record using a hashing algorithm. Then attempt Extension Activity 13B: write pseudocode/program to simulate a name-based hashing algorithm using ASCII values

LO.text: Students will be able to explain binary floating-point representation using mantissa and exponent (M × 2^E)
Students will be able to convert a positive binary floating-point number into its denary equivalent using both methods

Activities.text: Starter: 'What You Should Already Know' — students attempt warm-up questions 1–4 on binary/two's complement conversions and binary addition (individual, 10 mins)
Teacher-led introduction to floating-point representation: why fixed-point is limited, introducing M × 2^E, mantissa and exponent bit layout (Figure 13.7)
Worked examples on the board: convert Examples 13.1 and 13.2 using both Method 1 (fraction arithmetic) and Method 2 (binary point shift) — students work alongside

Consolidation.text: Students independently convert one positive binary floating-point number using both methods and compare results — teacher checks for understanding of binary point shift

Homework.text: Activity 13F parts a–e — convert five binary floating-point numbers into denary using your preferred method; show all working

LO.text: Students will be able to convert a negative binary floating-point number into denary using two's complement
Students will be able to complete Activity 13F across positive and negative examples

Activities.text: Recap: two volunteers demonstrate their Activity 13F solutions on the board — class checks and corrects
Teacher-led worked examples: Examples 13.3 and 13.4 (negative mantissa values) — demonstrating two's complement conversion of the mantissa before applying Method 2
Paired practice: Activity 13F parts f–j (negative values) — students work in pairs, comparing answers and identifying errors

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: if the mantissa starts with a 1 bit, what does this indicate? Walk through the steps to convert a negative mantissa — what must you do before shifting the binary point?

Homework.text: Activity 13F parts f–j if not completed in class. Write a step-by-step guide in your own words for converting a negative binary floating-point number into denary

LO.text: Students will be able to convert a positive denary number into binary floating-point representation using both methods
Students will be able to represent fractional denary values in binary floating-point format

Activities.text: Teacher-led worked examples: Example 13.5 (+4.5) and Example 13.6 (+0.171875) using both Method 1 (improper fraction) and Method 2 (binary conversion then binary point shift)
Class discussion: why must the mantissa start with 0.1 for a positive normalised number? (preview of normalisation)
Individual practice: Activity 13G Q2 parts a–e (convert positive denary numbers +3.5, 0.3125, 15.375, 41/64, 9.125 into binary floating-point)

Consolidation.text: Students check each other's answers for Activity 13G Q2 a–e and identify any steps where errors were made — teacher addresses common mistakes

Homework.text: Activity 13G Q1 parts a–e — convert the given fractions with exponents into binary floating-point format. Show all working clearly

LO.text: Students will be able to convert a negative denary number into binary floating-point representation
Students will be able to apply two's complement to the integer part before converting to floating-point format

Activities.text: Recap: quick-fire check — how do you convert a positive denary number to binary floating-point? (3-step summary on the board)
Teacher-led worked example: Example 13.7 (−10.375) using both methods — emphasising the two's complement step in Method 2 and the 1.0 mantissa format for negative numbers
Individual practice: Activity 13G Q2 parts f–j (negative denary conversions: −15/32, −3.5, −10.25, −1.046875, −3 11/32)

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: convert −6.5 into binary floating-point format (8-bit mantissa, 8-bit exponent) showing all steps — teacher marks on entry next lesson

Homework.text: Activity 13G Q1 parts f–j — convert negative fraction × exponent values into binary floating-point. Then attempt Extension Activity 13C: show why two given representations are equivalent

LO.text: Students will be able to explain what normalisation is and why it is needed
Students will be able to normalise a binary floating-point number by shifting the mantissa and adjusting the exponent

Activities.text: Starter: show Figure 13.8 from the textbook — four different representations of the number 2. Class discussion: why is this a problem? What rule could fix it?
Teacher-led explanation of normalisation rules: positive numbers must start 0.1, negative numbers must start 1.0; shift bits left, reduce exponent by the number of shifts
Worked examples: Examples 13.8 and 13.9 on the board (positive and negative normalisation), then students complete Activity 13H (normalise 10 floating-point numbers)

Consolidation.text: Traffic light self-assessment against the two LOs. Common error discussion: what happens to the exponent when you shift the mantissa left by 3 places?

Homework.text: Complete any remaining questions from Activity 13H. Write a brief explanation of why normalisation improves precision. Attempt Extension Activity 13F: how is zero represented in normalised floating-point? Research and explain

LO.text: Students will be able to explain overflow, underflow and rounding errors in floating-point representation
Students will be able to evaluate the trade-off between precision (mantissa size) and range (exponent size)

Activities.text: Teacher-led explanation using the 5.88 rounding example from section 13.3 — step-by-step binary approximation; result is stored as 5.75; discuss how extending the mantissa reduces error
Class discussion of overflow (result too large for word size) and underflow (result too small) using Activity 13I Q3 scenarios; introduce the special case of representing zero
Precision vs range: analyse Figures 13.10–13.16 — compare 12-bit mantissa/4-bit exponent vs 4-bit mantissa/12-bit exponent; Activity 13I Q1, Q2 and Q4

Consolidation.text: End-of-chapter exam question 1 (parts a i, a ii) — students attempt under timed conditions (12 minutes), then peer-mark using class discussion

Homework.text: Complete end-of-chapter question 1 in full. Write a paragraph evaluating: if a computer doubles its mantissa size from 16 to 32 bits but keeps the same total word length, what are the consequences for precision and range?

LO.text: Students will be able to distinguish between system software and application software
Students will be able to identify examples of common types of application software and their functions

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains the software/hardware hierarchy using Figure 4.1 and Figure 4.2, then introduces the general features of system software vs application software
We do: Class works through the Figure 4.3 examples together (word processor, spreadsheet, database, apps), agreeing as a group on the main function of each
You do: Students independently research and describe one further application software example not covered in class, stating its typical functions

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: give one example of system software and one example of application software, and explain the key difference between them

Homework.text: Sketch your own version of Figure 4.2, sorting 8 pieces of software you use at home or school into system software and application software

LO.text: Students will be able to compare command line interfaces and graphical user interfaces
Students will be able to describe the memory management and security management functions of an operating system

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains CLI and GUI using Table 4.1 and Figures 4.8/4.9, then explains memory management and security management from Figure 4.7
We do: Class discusses, as a group, who would use a CLI versus a GUI and why, then works through what could go wrong if two applications used the same memory location
You do: Students independently complete a comparison table listing at least two advantages and two disadvantages of CLI and GUI, in their own words

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: name one function of memory management and one function of security management in an operating system

Homework.text: Write a paragraph explaining, using Table 4.1, which type of interface (CLI or GUI) would be more suitable for a professional programmer and which for an everyday computer user, and why

LO.text: Students will be able to describe hardware peripheral management, file management, multitasking and user account management in an operating system

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains hardware peripheral management using the printer buffer/queue example, then file management tasks and multitasking (Figure 4.10)
We do: Class puts the steps of the printer management sequence in the correct order together (driver loaded, data to buffer, queue if busy, control commands, error handling)
You do: Students independently complete Activity 4.1 Q1 — the system vs application software table

Consolidation.text: Traffic light self-assessment: can students name all nine functions of an operating system shown in Figure 4.7?

Homework.text: Choose four features of an operating system and describe their function (Activity 4.1 Q3)

LO.text: Students will be able to describe the role of the BIOS and firmware when a computer starts up
Students will be able to explain what an interrupt is and how buffers are used alongside interrupts

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains booting up, BIOS/firmware and EEPROM/CMOS using Figure 4.11, then explains interrupts and buffers using Figures 4.12 and 4.13 (the printer example)
We do: Class sequences the steps of Figure 4.13 together as a group, explaining what happens when the printer buffer becomes empty
You do: Students independently complete Activity 4.1 Q2 (the video-freezing/printing interrupt scenario) and Q4-5 (descriptors and BIOS)

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: explain, in your own words, why buffers and interrupts prevent the microprocessor sitting idle while a document prints

Homework.text: Complete Activity 4.1 Q6 (matching descriptions to computer terms) if not finished in class

LO.text: Students will be able to recall the functions of money and of commercial/central banks (Chapter 16)
Students will be able to recall the key influences on household spending, saving and borrowing (Chapter 17)

Activities.text: I do: Teacher recaps the Chapter 16 summary points (the four functions of money, what makes an item suitable as money, functions of commercial and central banks) and the Chapter 17 summary points (influences on spending, saving and borrowing)
We do: Class works through Chapter 16's four-part question part (b) together — explaining two functions of a central bank — agreeing on a model answer as a group
You do: Students independently attempt the Chapter 16 and Chapter 17 multiple choice questions (4 each) and mark their own answers against the answer key

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: name the four functions of money and one function of a central bank not yet mentioned this lesson

Homework.text: Attempt the Chapter 17 four-part question in full (a-d), covering the opportunity cost of saving through to whether income always affects spending

LO.text: Students will be able to recall the wage and non-wage factors affecting occupational choice and earnings (Chapter 18)
Students will be able to recall how trade unions negotiate pay and working conditions (Chapter 19)

Activities.text: I do: Teacher recaps the Chapter 18 summary points (demand/supply of labour, elasticity, division of labour) and the Chapter 19 summary points (trade union types, collective bargaining, factors affecting union strength)
We do: Class works through Section 3's cumulative Q5 together (which combination of productivity and unemployment increases a trade union's bargaining power), agreeing on the reasoning as a group
You do: Students independently attempt the Chapter 18 and Chapter 19 multiple choice questions and check their answers

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: give one factor that increases the demand for a worker's labour, and one factor that increases a trade union's bargaining strength

Homework.text: Attempt the Chapter 19 four-part question in full, explaining why trade union membership may decline and analysing the factors that influence a union's strength

LO.text: Students will be able to recall why firms grow, the types of merger, and economies/diseconomies of scale (Chapter 20)
Students will be able to recall the factors influencing the choice between labour-intensive and capital-intensive production (Chapter 21)

Activities.text: I do: Teacher recaps the Chapter 20 summary points (reasons for firm size, types of merger, internal and external economies/diseconomies of scale) and the Chapter 21 summary points (factors of production, capital- vs labour-intensive production)
We do: Class works through Chapter 20's four-part question part (c) together — analysing two internal economies of scale — agreeing on a model answer as a group
You do: Students independently attempt the Chapter 20 and Chapter 21 multiple choice questions and check their answers

Consolidation.text: Traffic light self-assessment: can students name the three types of merger and give one example of an internal economy of scale?

Homework.text: Attempt the Chapter 21 four-part question in full, analysing why car production has become more capital-intensive and discussing whether this increases unemployment

LO.text: Students will be able to recall how firms' costs, revenue and profit are calculated and the key features of competitive markets and monopoly (Chapters 22-23)
Students will be able to apply Section 3 concepts to cumulative exam-style questions

Activities.text: I do: Teacher recaps the Chapter 22 summary points (fixed/variable costs, revenue, profit maximisation) and the Chapter 23 summary points (competitive markets vs monopoly, barriers to entry)

We do: Class works through Section 3's cumulative Q6-8 together (the profit-maximising output, the variable cost diagram, calculating profit from price/AFC/AVC), agreeing on each calculation as a group
You do: Students independently attempt the remaining Section 3 cumulative multiple choice questions (Q1-5, Q9-10) covering the whole of Chapters 16-23

Consolidation.text: Whole-class review of the cumulative multiple choice answers, with students justifying their reasoning for the profit-maximisation and monopoly questions

Homework.text: Attempt the Section 3 data-response question on corporate lawyers' wages, using it to revise the influences on earnings covered in Chapter 18

LO.text: Students will be able to define utility, total utility and marginal utility
Students will be able to explain the law of diminishing marginal utility using real-world examples

Activities.text: Starter: Black Friday discussion — why do shoppers queue overnight for deals? What satisfaction are they seeking? (5 mins)
Teacher-led explanation of utility, total utility and marginal utility using the pizza slice example from the textbook
Paired task: students generate their own real-world example of diminishing marginal utility and share with the class

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: define total utility and marginal utility in your own words and give one personal example of the law of diminishing marginal utility

Homework.text: Read Chapter 30.1 and complete Activity 30.1 — calculate marginal utility for each day of revision and draw both the total utility and marginal utility curves

LO.text: Students will be able to calculate total utility and marginal utility from a data table
Students will be able to draw and interpret total utility and marginal utility curves

Activities.text: Recap quiz: key definitions from last lesson (3 quick-fire questions)
Worked example on the board: calculating TU and MU from a data set, then plotting both curves
Individual task: students complete their own TU/MU table and graphs using a new data set (food/drink scenario)

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: what happens to MU as consumption increases? At what point does TU reach its maximum? What does it mean when MU is negative?

Homework.text: Past paper multiple choice questions on utility and diminishing marginal utility — minimum 5 questions with written justifications

LO.text: Students will be able to explain the equi-marginal principle and define consumer equilibrium
Students will be able to apply the MU/P formula to determine a consumer's optimal spending allocation

Activities.text: Starter: think-pair-share — if you had $10 to spend on two goods, how would you decide how much of each to buy?
Teacher-led explanation of the equi-marginal principle using Table 30.2 (products x and y)
Small group task: Activity 30.2 — students choose three items, estimate MU/P for each, and compare rational vs intuitive ranking

Consolidation.text: Traffic light self-assessment: can students write the equi-marginal condition formula from memory and explain what each term means?

Homework.text: Complete a structured question: given a table of MU values and prices for two goods and a fixed income, calculate the consumer equilibrium and explain your working

LO.text: Students will be able to use the equi-marginal principle to derive an individual demand curve
Students will be able to explain how a price change shifts consumer equilibrium and increases quantity demanded

Activities.text: Recap: using Table 30.2 from last lesson, teacher models what happens when the price of product y falls from $2 to $1 — show how MU/P changes and a new equilibrium is reached
Students complete Activity 30.3: justify the new consumer equilibrium, calculate the increase in total utility, and discuss how to derive a more complete demand curve
Class discussion: how does this utility-based derivation relate to the standard downward-sloping demand curve?

Consolidation.text: Students sketch the derived individual demand curve for product y (Figure 30.3 style) and annotate it with labels explaining the link to marginal utility

Homework.text: Exam-style short answer: explain, using marginal utility theory, why a consumer buys more of a good when its price falls. (8 marks)

LO.text: Students will be able to evaluate the limitations of marginal utility theory
Students will be able to assess the assumption of rational behaviour and consider real-world challenges to it

Activities.text: Starter: 'Think Like an Economist' — discuss the increase in tinned food sales in the UK. Does this fit with utility theory?
Teacher-led discussion of the four key assumptions of marginal utility theory and why each is problematic in the real world
Debate activity: half the class defends utility theory as a useful model; the other half argues it is too unrealistic — structured 10-minute debate

Consolidation.text: Knowledge organiser completion: students fill in a summary table of utility theory — key terms, assumptions, strengths, and limitations

Homework.text: Read ahead on behavioural economics (any supplementary notes provided). Write a short paragraph explaining one real-world example where consumers do NOT behave rationally and link it to a limitation of utility theory

LO.text: Students will be able to apply utility theory concepts to exam-style multiple choice and structured questions
Students will be able to identify command words and structure answers to utility questions under timed conditions

Activities.text: Timed multiple choice practice: end-of-chapter questions 1–3 (individual, 10 mins) followed by class review of answers and common misconceptions
Paired exam question: 'Explain, using the equi-marginal principle, how a rational consumer allocates their income between two goods' — students mark each other's responses using a mark scheme

Consolidation.text: Class discussion: what are the most common mistakes on utility questions? Teacher compiles a 'watch out for' list on the board

Homework.text: Complete a full past paper structured question on utility and marginal utility under timed conditions (20 minutes). Self-mark using the mark scheme

LO.text: Students will be able to consolidate and self-evaluate their understanding of all Chapter 30 learning objectives
Students will be able to identify remaining gaps in their knowledge and plan targeted revision

Activities.text: Self-evaluation using the Chapter 30 checklist (textbook p.XXX) — students RAG-rate each learning objective
Flashcard activity: students create revision cards for every key term and concept in Chapter 30
Peer teaching: students who are confident on a topic explain it to a partner who has identified it as a weakness

Consolidation.text: Cold-call round: each student asked one question from the chapter — teacher uses self-evaluation data to target questions at individual students

Homework.text: Revise Chapter 30 using your self-evaluation checklist as a guide. Attempt any end-of-chapter questions you have not yet completed. Prepare for a short written test next lesson

LO.text: Students will be able to explain what a user-defined data type is and distinguish between non-composite and composite data types
Students will be able to define and use an enumerated data type in pseudocode

Activities.text: Starter: attempt the two 'What You Should Already Know' questions (selecting appropriate data types; writing a record structure for a zoo animal), then discuss as a class

Teacher-led explanation of user-defined data types and the non-composite/composite distinction, then introduce enumerated data types using the Tmonth example (declaring thisMonth/nextMonth and incrementing nextMonth)
Individual task: Activity 13A — declare an enumerated type for the days of the week, declare today/yesterday variables, assign Wednesday to today, and write the assignment statement for tomorrow

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: in your own words, what is the difference between a non-composite and a composite data type? Give one example of each

Homework.text: Write pseudocode to declare an enumerated type for the four seasons of the year, declare two variables of that type, and write assignment statements to set and increment them

LO.text: Students will be able to define and use a pointer data type in pseudocode, including dereferencing

Activities.text: Recap quiz: what is an enumerated data type? (cold-call, 2 questions)
Teacher-led explanation of pointer data types using the TmonthPointer example — declaring the pointer type, setting monthPointer to ^thisMonth, and dereferencing with monthPointer^
Individual task: Activity 13B — declare a pointer to the days-of-the-week enumerated type from last lesson and set it to point at today

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: what does the ^ symbol mean when declaring a pointer type versus when dereferencing a pointer variable?

Homework.text: Write pseudocode to declare a pointer type for the seasons enumerated type from last lesson's homework, declare a pointer variable, and use it to point at and then dereference a season value

LO.text: Students will be able to define and use composite data types including records, sets and classes
Students will be able to choose and justify an appropriate user-defined data type for a given problem

Activities.text: Teacher-led recap of records as a composite data type (linking back to Chapter 10), using the TbookRecord example
Teacher-led explanation of sets using the Sletter/vowel example, and a brief introduction to classes as composite data types (linking forward to Chapter 20)

LO.text: Students will be able to convert between hexadecimal and denary numbers in both directions

Activities.text: Recap: quick-fire round converting a few binary numbers to hex using Table 1.1
Teacher-led worked examples: Example 1 (hex 4 5 A) and Example 2 (hex C 8 F) — converting hex to denary by multiplying each digit by its heading value
Teacher-led worked examples: Example 1 (denary 2004) and Example 2 (denary 8463) — converting denary to hex using successive division by 16 (Figures 1.2a and 1.2b)
Individual practice: Activity 1.5 (hex to denary) and Activity 1.6 (denary to hex)

Consolidation.text: Mini whiteboard check: convert one new hexadecimal number to denary and hold up the answer

Homework.text: Complete any remaining parts of Activities 1.5 and 1.6

LO.text: Students will be able to describe real-world uses of the hexadecimal system

Activities.text: Teacher-led explanation of why hexadecimal is more convenient for humans than binary, using the D2AF example

Teacher-led tour of four real-world uses of hex: error codes (Figure 1.3), MAC addresses (the NN-NN-NN-DD-DD-DD format and manufacturer codes), IPv6 addresses, and HTML colour codes (Figures 1.4 and 1.5, the #RRGGBB format)
Paired task: Activity 1.7 — identify colours from given RGB denary values and convert them into hexadecimal

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: give one real-world example of where you might see a hexadecimal value used, and explain what it represents

Homework.text: Find the MAC address of one of your own devices (or research an example) and explain, using this chapter, what the two halves of the address represent

LO.text: Students will be able to add two 8-bit positive binary numbers, using carry and sum correctly

Activities.text: Teacher-led recap of denary column addition (97 + 64) to introduce the idea of carry and sum, then the binary addition rules table (0+0, 0+1, 1+0, 1+1)
Teacher-led worked examples: Example 1 (00100111 + 01001010) and Example 2 (126 + 62 converted to binary then added, checked against the denary sum)
Paired practice: Activity 1.8 (binary addition) and Activity 1.9 (convert denary pairs to binary, add, and check against the denary sum)

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: add 00010011 + 00010001 showing your carry and sum rows, and state the denary equivalent of your answer

Homework.text: Complete any remaining parts of Activities 1.8 and 1.9

LO.text: Students will be able to explain what an overflow error is and identify when one has occurred in binary addition

Activities.text: Recap: two volunteers demonstrate an Activity 1.9 answer on the board
Teacher-led worked example: Example 3 (01101110 + 11011110) — showing the 9th bit generated and why the 8-bit answer (76) doesn't match the true denary sum (332)
Class discussion: what is the maximum denary value of an 8-bit, 16-bit and 32-bit register, and why does exceeding it cause overflow?
Individual task: Activity 1.10 — add the given denary pairs as 8-bit and 16-bit binary numbers and comment on whether overflow has occurred

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: how can you tell, just by looking at your working, that an 8-bit binary addition has overflowed?

Homework.text: Complete any remaining parts of Activity 1.10, and write one sentence explaining why increasing the register size (e.g. from 8-bit to 16-bit) reduces the chance of overflow

LO.text: Students will be able to explain the differences between the internet and the World Wide Web
Students will be able to identify the components of a URL and explain the purpose of HTTP and HTTPS

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains the difference between the internet and the WWW using Table 5.1, then breaks down the structure of a URL (protocol://website address/path/file name) using the hoddereducation.co.uk example
We do: Class works through identifying the domain host, domain name, domain type and file name in a new example URL together, agreeing on each part as a group
You do: Students independently complete Activity 5.1 Q1 — identifying the domain name, domain type, file name and protocol from a given URL

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: what does the 's' in https stand for, and why does it matter when entering personal or payment details on a website?

Homework.text: Find three URLs you use regularly (e.g. school website, a shopping site, a streaming service) and break each one down into its protocol, domain host, domain name, domain type and path

LO.text: Students will be able to describe the main features of a web browser
Students will be able to explain how DNS locates a web page and distinguish between session and persistent cookies

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains web browser features (Figures 5.1/5.2) and demonstrates how DNS locates a web page step by step using Figure 5.3
We do: Class sequences the five steps of Figure 5.3 together, explaining what happens at each numbered stage as a group
You do: Students independently complete Activity 5.1 Q2 — describing two differences between session and persistent cookies and three uses of cookies

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: why might a website use a persistent cookie rather than a session cookie for a login system?

Homework.text: Complete Activity 5.1 Q3 and Q4 — sorting internet/WWW features and explaining why persistent cookies are sometimes called tracking cookies

LO.text: Students will be able to explain what digital currency and cryptocurrency are
Students will be able to describe how blockchaining secures a chain of transactions

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains digital currency and centralisation (Figure 5.6), then cryptocurrency and decentralisation (Figure 5.7), then how a blockchain is built from linked blocks (Figures 5.8/5.9)
We do: Class traces what happens if block 2 in Figure 5.9 is changed, working through as a group why blocks 3 onwards become invalid
You do: Students independently complete Activity 5.2 — drawing a seven-block blockchain diagram and describing what would happen if block 4 was hacked

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: explain, in your own words, why proof-of-work makes it almost impossible to hack a blockchain

Homework.text: Complete Activity 5.2 Q2 — explain the main differences between digital currency and cryptocurrency

LO.text: Students will be able to describe brute force attacks, data interception and DDoS attacks as cyber security threats

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains brute force attacks (common password lists, word lists), data interception (packet sniffing, wardriving) and DDoS attacks (flooding a server with requests)
We do: Class discusses, as a group, why using public Wi-Fi at an airport is risky and what defences (WEP encryption, firewall) reduce that risk
You do: Students independently list the warning signs that a user has become the victim of a DDoS attack, using the textbook's list as a starting point

Consolidation.text: Mini whiteboard check: name one method a hacker could use to carry out a data interception attack

Homework.text: Explain, in your own words, why a distributed denial of service attack is harder to block than a regular denial of service attack

LO.text: Students will be able to distinguish between actual and potential economic growth
Students will be able to explain why governments aim for economic growth and how they set growth targets

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains actual vs potential economic growth using the production possibility curve (Figure 25.1, movement A to B vs the shift from YY to ZZ), then explains how AD and AS diagrams (Figures 25.2-25.4) show economic growth
We do: Class works through Group Activity 1 parts a and b together — interpreting Mexico's 2.1% economic growth rate and discussing what underemployment means
You do: Students independently complete Group Activity 1 parts c and d — identifying which sector had the highest underemployment and whether Mexico could have grown faster than 2.1%

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: explain the difference between actual economic growth and potential economic growth, using the production possibility curve

Homework.text: Explain, in your own words, two reasons why a government wants to achieve economic growth for its country

LO.text: Students will be able to calculate the unemployment rate and explain why governments aim for low unemployment
Students will be able to explain why governments aim for price stability rather than 0% inflation

Activities.text: I do: Teacher demonstrates calculating the unemployment rate using the 5 million/40 million example, then explains why governments aim for price stability and the two reasons they don't target 0% inflation
We do: Class works through calculating a new unemployment rate example together, then discusses South Africa's inflation target range (3-6%) from Individual Activity 1
You do: Students independently complete Individual Activity 1 — identifying a central bank function and commenting on how successful the South African Reserve Bank was at hitting its inflation target

Consolidation.text: Mini whiteboard check: calculate the unemployment rate for a labour force of 25 million with 2 million unemployed

Homework.text: Explain two reasons why measures of inflation tend to overstate rises in prices

LO.text: Students will be able to explain why governments aim for balance of payments stability
Students will be able to explain why and how governments redistribute income

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains balance of payments stability (export revenue vs import expenditure) and redistribution of income (taxing the rich, spending on the poor via benefits, education and health)
We do: Class works through Group Activity 2 part a together — discussing whether any of the five countries in the table achieved all their macroeconomic aims in 2016
You do: Students independently complete Group Activity 2 part b — identifying which country likely had the highest number of unemployed workers, explaining their answer

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: give one reason a government might not be concerned about a small, short-term balance of payments deficit

Homework.text: Explain two reasons why a government may want to redistribute income from the rich to the poor

LO.text: Students will be able to explain the possible conflicts between macroeconomic aims and how a government might prioritise between them

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains the conflict between full employment and price stability, and between growth/full employment and balance of payments stability
We do: Class discusses, as a group, how a government might decide between reducing inflation and reducing unemployment when the aims conflict
You do: Students independently attempt the chapter's four multiple choice questions and mark their own answers

Consolidation.text: Whole-class review of the multiple choice answers, with students justifying their reasoning for Q2 (the unemployment rate calculation) and Q4 (potential growth)

Homework.text: Attempt the chapter's four-part question in full (a-d), from identifying two macroeconomic aims through to discussing whether all governments share the same economic aims

LO.text: Students will be able to define economic efficiency and distinguish between productive and allocative efficiency

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains the concept of economic efficiency stemming from the fundamental economic problem, then defines productive efficiency (lowest possible cost) and allocative efficiency (producing what consumers most want) using the car assembly plant example

We do: Class discusses, as a group, the 'Economics in context' case study on aircraft fuel efficiency (Figure 32.2) — identifying the implications for airlines and other ways aircraft could be used more efficiently
You do: Students independently choose one of the chapter's real-world examples (oil, timber, water or trade) and explain, in writing, why it represents an efficiency problem

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: in one sentence each, define productive efficiency and allocative efficiency

Homework.text: Find a recent news example of inefficient use of a scarce resource in your own country and explain whether it relates to productive or allocative inefficiency

LO.text: Students will be able to explain the conditions needed for productive efficiency using an average cost curve and a production possibility curve

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains productive efficiency using the average cost curve (Figure 32.3) and the production possibility curve (Figure 32.4, points X and Y), then demonstrates how competition forces firms towards the lowest point on their average cost curve (Figure 32.5)
We do: Class discusses, as a group, why point X inside the PPC represents productive inefficiency while point Y on the boundary represents productive efficiency
You do: Students independently sketch a PPC and label a point of productive efficiency and a point of productive inefficiency, explaining their choice

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: why does competition push firms towards producing at the lowest point on their average cost curve?

Homework.text: Explain, in your own words, why a firm that fails to minimise its costs in a competitive market risks bankruptcy

LO.text: Students will be able to explain the conditions needed for allocative efficiency, including price equal to marginal cost

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains allocative efficiency (price = marginal cost) using Table 32.1, demonstrating why outputs of 1-3 and 5-7 units are not allocatively efficient but 4 units is
We do: Class works through Activity 32.1 Q1 together, deciding which type of efficiency each of the four scenarios leads towards
You do: Students independently complete Activity 32.1 Q2 — discussing, in a group, how online shopping could lead to greater efficiency in global markets, and making a poster of their findings

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: using Table 32.1, explain why an output of 4 units is the only allocatively efficient output level

Homework.text: Explain how a competitive market forces firms towards allocative efficiency, referencing Figure 32.5

LO.text: Students will be able to explain the concept of Pareto optimality and apply it to a real-world example

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains Pareto optimality using the PPC (Figure 32.4) and the Istanbul airport expansion example (who gains, who loses, compensation)
We do: Class discusses, as a group, whether point X within the PPC represents a Pareto-inefficient allocation and what a Pareto improvement would look like
You do: Students independently complete Activity 32.2 — choosing an example from their own country to explain Pareto optimality and producing a poster

Consolidation.text: Traffic light self-assessment: can students explain what a Pareto improvement is, using the airport expansion example?

Homework.text: Explain why residents living near an expanded airport might be considered 'worse off', and why compensation may not always resolve this

LO.text: Students will be able to explain the concept of dynamic efficiency and how it benefits a firm over time

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains dynamic efficiency using the long-run average cost curve shift (Figure 32.6) and the motor vehicle manufacturing industry example (from Henry Ford to modern automation)
We do: Class discusses, as a group, why investment in dynamic efficiency can result in higher costs initially before benefits are seen later
You do: Students independently complete Activity 32.3 — explaining how the food processing industry, livestock farming or courier services could achieve dynamic efficiency

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: what happens to a firm's long-run average cost curve when it achieves dynamic efficiency?

Homework.text: Compare and contrast productive efficiency and dynamic efficiency in a short paragraph

LO.text: Students will be able to define market failure and identify its main causes

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains market failure as markets failing to deliver efficiency, then introduces the six causes (externalities, merit/demerit goods, public/quasi-public goods, information failure, adverse selection/moral hazard, monopoly power)

We do: Class works through the 'Think like an economist' case study on flying less together, discussing the likely economic and social impact of fewer people flying and the effect on global supply chains
You do: Students independently choose two of the six causes of market failure and give a real-world example of each

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: name three of the six causes of market failure covered in this lesson

Homework.text: Research one example of market failure in your own country and identify which of the six causes it relates to

LO.text: Students will be able to apply Chapter 32 concepts to exam-style multiple choice questions and self-assess their understanding of efficiency and market failure

Activities.text: I do: Teacher reviews the chapter's key concepts using the self-evaluation checklist, recapping productive efficiency, allocative efficiency, Pareto optimality, dynamic efficiency and market failure
We do: Class works through exam-style multiple choice Questions 1 and 2 together, agreeing on the correct answer and reasoning as a group
You do: Students independently attempt exam-style multiple choice Questions 3, 4 and 5 under timed conditions, then peer-mark

Consolidation.text: Whole-class review of the multiple choice answers, with students justifying their reasoning for Q2 (the PPC movement) and Q5 (identifying market failure)

Homework.text: Complete the chapter's self-evaluation checklist, rating yourself against each learning intention, and note one topic from this chapter you still need to revise

LO.text: Students will be able to explain why protocols are needed for communication over networks
Students will be able to describe the four-layer structure of TCP/IP protocols

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains why protocols are essential using the parity checking example (agreeing even/odd parity), then introduces the four-layer TCP/IP structure (Figure 14.1) and the concept of decomposition
We do: Class works through 'What you should already know' Q1 together, explaining IP, TCP and why protocols are used
You do: Students independently answer 'What you should already know' Q2-3, explaining peer-to-peer networks and the terms stack/queue

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: name the four layers of TCP/IP in the order data travels when sending, and again for receiving

Homework.text: Explain, in your own words, why using layers (decomposition) makes it easier to develop network software and hardware

LO.text: Students will be able to describe the role of the application layer and explain how HTTP retrieves a web page

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains the application layer and its protocols (Table 14.1), then demonstrates the HTTP request/response process using Figure 14.2 and the step-by-step summary
We do: Class sequences the HTTP steps together (URL entered, HTTP to TCP, DNS lookup, acknowledgement, HTML returned, browser displays), checking the order as a group
You do: Students independently write out, in their own words, the full sequence of events when a user requests a web page, from typing the URL to the page displaying

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: what role does the DNS server play when a browser requests a web page?

Homework.text: Explain the difference between the application layer's role and the transport layer's role in sending a web page request

LO.text: Students will be able to describe the file transfer protocol (FTP) and its main features

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains FTP, comparing it to HTTP and SMTP, then demonstrates anonymous FTP, FTP commands (delete, close, rename, cd, lcd) and the FTP server using the ftp://username@ftp.example.gov/ example
We do: Class works through a scenario together — deciding which FTP commands would be needed to log in, navigate to a folder and download a file
You do: Students independently write a short explanation of when a business might use FTP rather than HTTP to transfer files

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: what is the difference between a named FTP login and an anonymous FTP login?

Homework.text: Research one real-world use of FTP and explain why FTP was chosen over other methods of file transfer

LO.text: Students will be able to explain the SMTP protocol and why MIME is needed for email attachments

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains SMTP as a text-based push protocol, then explains why MIME is needed for binary file attachments (images, video, music) using the MIME header example
We do: Class discusses, as a group, why SMTP alone cannot handle an email with a photo attachment, and how MIME solves this
You do: Students independently write a short explanation comparing a 'push' protocol to what they predict a 'pull' protocol might mean, ready for next lesson

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: why is SMTP described as a push protocol?

Homework.text: Explain what would happen if a user tried to email a video file using only SMTP without MIME

LO.text: Students will be able to compare POP3/4 and IMAP and explain the concept of pull protocols

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains POP3/4 and IMAP as pull protocols using Figures 14.3 and 14.4, then demonstrates the synchronisation difference between them using Table 14.2
We do: Class decides, as a group, whether POP3/4 or IMAP would be better for a user who checks email on multiple devices, justifying their choice using Table 14.2
You do: Students independently complete Activity 14A Q1c — describing the use of protocols when sending and receiving emails and the difference between SMTP and MIME

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: if a user deletes an email on their phone using IMAP, what happens to the copy on the server compared to using POP3/4?

Homework.text: Complete Activity 14A Q1a and Q1b — naming the four TCP/IP layers and one protocol associated with each

LO.text: Students will be able to explain how TCP ensures the safe, ordered delivery of data using host-to-host communication

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains TCP's role (positive acknowledgement with re-transmission, connection-oriented handshake) and demonstrates the host-to-host handshake steps between hosts X and Y

We do: Class sequences the four handshake steps together (X sends a segment with sync bits, Y responds with acknowledgement and its own sync bits, X acknowledges, transmission begins), checking the order as a group
You do: Students independently draw a labelled diagram showing the TCP handshake between two named hosts

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: what does PAR stand for, and why is it important for TCP?

Homework.text: Explain why TCP is often referred to as a 'host-to-host' transmission protocol

LO.text: Students will be able to describe the role of the internet/network layer and the structure of an Ethernet frame

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains the internet layer's functions (routing, IP header, datagram to frame) and demonstrates the Ethernet frame structure using Figure 14.5
We do: Class labels a copy of Figure 14.5 together, identifying the destination, source, Ethernet type/length, data and frame check fields
You do: Students independently complete Activity 14A Q2a and Q2b — explaining what Ethernet is and describing the contents of an Ethernet frame

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: what is stored in the 'frame check' field of an Ethernet frame, and what is it used for?

Homework.text: Complete Activity 14A Q2c — explain how external devices can be communicated with when using Ethernet, given that Ethernet alone cannot do this

LO.text: Students will be able to perform a logical left shift on an 8-bit binary number and explain its effect

Activities.text: Teacher-led explanation of logical shifts — each left shift multiplies the binary value by 2, with empty positions filled with 0
Teacher-led worked example: Example 1 (denary 21, shifting 1, 2, 3 and 4 places left), showing how the 4-place shift causes the most significant bit to be lost and produces an incorrect result
Individual practice: attempt the left-shift parts of Activity 1.11 Q1, checking denary values before and after each shift

Consolidation.text: Mini whiteboard check: shift 00010101 two places left, write the new 8-bit value and its denary equivalent

Homework.text: Using the worked Example 1 as a model, shift the binary value for denary 30 two places left, showing the register before and after, and state what multiplication this represents

LO.text: Students will be able to perform a logical right shift on an 8-bit binary number and explain the effect of shifting in either direction

Activities.text: Recap: quick-fire question on what a left shift represents mathematically
Teacher-led worked example: Example 2 (denary 200, shifting 1, 2, 3 and 4 places right), showing how the least significant bit is lost after too many right shifts
Teacher-led worked examples: Example 3 and Example 4 — combining binary addition with a subsequent left or right shift
Individual practice: Activity 1.11 Q2 — convert 29 and 51 to binary, add them, then shift the result right and left as instructed

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: explain, using Example 2, why shifting 200 four places right does not give the mathematically correct answer

Homework.text: Complete any remaining parts of Activity 1.11

LO.text: Students will be able to write positive binary numbers in two's complement format and convert them back into denary

Activities.text: Teacher-led introduction to two's complement — the −128 column heading and how the left-most bit indicates the sign of the number
Teacher-led worked examples: writing positive denary numbers 19, 4, 38 and 125 in two's complement format, and converting positive two's complement binary numbers (01101110, 00111111) back to denary
Individual practice: Activity 1.12 — convert the given positive denary numbers into 8-bit two's complement binary, and convert the given two's complement binary numbers into positive denary

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: in an 8-bit two's complement number, what does a 0 in the left-most (−128) column always tell you about the number?

Homework.text: Complete any remaining parts of Activity 1.12

LO.text: Students will be able to write negative binary numbers in two's complement format and convert negative denary numbers using both the direct method and the invert-and-add-one method

Activities.text: Teacher-led worked examples converting the two's complement binary numbers representing −109, −28 and −11 back to denary using the −128 column

Teacher-led worked examples: converting −67 and −79 into two's complement binary using Method 1 (placing 1s directly) and Method 2 (invert the positive binary and add 1), plus the 4-bit and 12-bit register examples
Individual practice: Activity 1.13 (negative denary to two's complement binary) and Activity 1.14 (two's complement binary to negative denary)

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: convert −18 into an 8-bit two's complement binary number using the invert-and-add-one method, showing all three steps

Homework.text: Complete any remaining parts of Activities 1.13 and 1.14, then write a short paragraph comparing the 'placing 1s directly' method and the 'invert and add 1' method for finding a negative binary number — which do you find more reliable, and why?

LO.text: Students will be able to explain what hacking is and describe the six types of malware covered in this chapter

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains hacking (illegal vs ethical), then demonstrates the six malware types using Figure 5.10 and Table 5.2 (viruses, worms, Trojan horses, spyware, adware, ransomware)
We do: Class works through comparing a virus and a worm together, agreeing as a group on the key difference (the need for an active host program)
You do: Students independently complete Activity 5.3 Q2 — explaining the terms worm, ransomware and Trojan horse

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: which type of malware needs an active host program to run, and which can spread through a network without one?

Homework.text: Complete Activity 5.3 Q3 — evaluate John's three password choices and describe how he could improve and maintain his passwords

LO.text: Students will be able to describe phishing, pharming and social engineering, and explain how each can be prevented

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains phishing (fake emails/links), pharming (DNS cache poisoning) and social engineering using Figures 5.11 and 5.12 (the five types of threat and four-stage scam process)
We do: Class discusses, as a group, which of the three human emotions (fear, curiosity, trust) each of the five social engineering examples in Figure 5.11 exploits
You do: Students independently complete Activity 5.3 Q1 — describing three data security issues a company might face and how to mitigate each

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: what is the key difference between phishing and pharming in terms of what action the user needs to take?

Homework.text: Research the term 'spear phishing' and explain, in your own words, how it differs from regular phishing

LO.text: Students will be able to explain how access levels and authentication (passwords, biometrics, two-step verification) keep data safe

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains access levels (hospital/social media examples) and the three authentication factors, then demonstrates biometric techniques using Table 5.3 and two-step verification using Figure 5.17
We do: Class works through evaluating the five passwords in Activity 5.4 Q1 together, agreeing as a group on which are strong and which are weak
You do: Students independently complete Activity 5.5 — describing how a face recognition system would differ from the retina scan example, and naming other biometric devices

Consolidation.text: Traffic light self-assessment: can students name the three authentication factors and give an example of each?

Homework.text: Complete Activity 5.4 Q2 — describe how an airport could control access levels for staff and customers, and guard against malware attacks

LO.text: Students will be able to identify the warning signs of a scam email and describe how firewalls, proxy servers, privacy settings and SSL keep data safe

Activities.text: I do: Teacher demonstrates spotting a scam email using Figures 5.19 and 5.20 (spelling, tone, suspicious links), then explains firewalls (Figure 5.21), proxy servers (Figure 5.22) and SSL (Figure 5.23)
We do: Class works through finding the errors in the sample PayPal scam email (Figure 5.19) together as a group
You do: Students independently complete Activity 5.6 Q1 — matching computer terms to their descriptions, and Q3 — identifying problems with the Watson, Williams and Co email

Consolidation.text: Whole-class review of the chapter's key terms list — students self-check which cyber security terms they can define confidently

Homework.text: Complete Activity 5.6 Q2 — describe how SSL and TLS certificates ensure secure data sharing between a browser and a website

LO.text: Students will be able to define a budget deficit, surplus and balanced budget
Students will be able to explain the four reasons why governments spend money, including the multiplier effect

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains the budget (deficit, surplus, balanced budget) and the four reasons for government spending, then demonstrates the multiplier effect using the $20m government spending example
We do: Class works through Individual Activity 1a together — calculating how much the Maldivian government was expected to spend in 2016 given its budget deficit and revenue forecast
You do: Students independently complete Individual Activity 1b — explaining how a decline in tourism would affect the Maldives' budget position

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: what is the difference between a budget deficit and a budget surplus?

Homework.text: Explain, in your own words, why the multiplier effect makes government spending 'a powerful government measure'

LO.text: Students will be able to explain the reasons governments levy taxes
Students will be able to distinguish between direct/indirect taxes and progressive/proportional/regressive taxes

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains the reasons for levying taxation, then the direct/indirect distinction and progressive/proportional/regressive taxes using Table 26.1
We do: Class works through Individual Activity 2 parts a and b together — deciding whether a tax on plastic carrier bags is direct or indirect, and identifying another reason for imposing it
You do: Students independently complete Individual Activity 2 part c — using a demand and supply diagram to explain the effect of a tax on plastic carrier bags on their market

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: is income tax usually progressive, proportional or regressive, and why?

Homework.text: Complete Group Activity 1 — explain why a government might charge oil firms a higher corporation tax rate, and whether Egypt's 2016 income tax system was progressive or regressive

LO.text: Students will be able to explain the qualities of a good tax
Students will be able to explain how price elasticity of demand and supply affect the incidence of an indirect tax

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains the six principles of a good tax (equity, certainty, convenience, economy, flexibility, efficiency), then demonstrates the incidence of taxation using Figure 26.1 (inelastic vs elastic demand)
We do: Class compares the tax burden shown in Figure 26.1(a) and (b) together, agreeing as a group on why consumers bear more of the tax when demand is inelastic
You do: Students independently complete Individual Activity 3 — explaining whether France's shift from income tax to VAT made its tax system more or less progressive

Consolidation.text: Traffic light self-assessment: can students name three qualities of a good tax and explain what each means?

Homework.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of relying on indirect taxes rather than direct taxes as a source of government revenue

LO.text: Students will be able to calculate a government's budget position from spending and revenue data
Students will be able to explain how expansionary and contractionary fiscal policy affect macroeconomic aims

Activities.text: I do: Teacher demonstrates calculating a budget balance and explains expansionary vs contractionary fiscal policy using Figure 26.2
We do: Class works through Individual Activity 4 parts a and b together — calculating New Zealand's 2016 budget position and identifying a form of spending on a public good
You do: Students independently complete Individual Activity 4 part c and attempt the chapter's four multiple choice questions

Consolidation.text: Whole-class review of the multiple choice answers, with students justifying their reasoning for Q3 (PED/PES and tax incidence) and Q4 (reading the tax diagram)

Homework.text: Attempt the chapter's four-part question in full (a-d), from defining a progressive tax through to discussing whether raising income tax rates will improve economic welfare

LO.text: Students will be able to define an externality and distinguish between negative and positive externalities

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains the concept of externalities and third parties using the flight path noise, chemical factory, vaccine research and flood barrier examples, then explains the negative/positive distinction

We do: Class discusses, as a group, the 'Economics in context' case study on air quality in Southeast Asia — identifying which groups are affected by the illegal burning of rainforest and why it is an example of market failure
You do: Students independently complete Activity 33.1 — explaining, for each of the four opening examples, why it involves an externality and whether it is negative or positive

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: in your own words, explain what a 'third party' is in the context of an externality

Homework.text: Find one example, not already covered in class, of a negative externality and one example of a positive externality, explaining who the third party is in each case

LO.text: Students will be able to define and calculate private, external and social costs and benefits

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains private costs/benefits, external costs/benefits and social costs/benefits using the airport expansion example, demonstrating the formulas Social costs = Private costs + External costs and Social benefits = Private benefits + External benefits
We do: Class works through Figure 33.3 together, identifying the private cost, external cost and social cost shown for the car journey example
You do: Students independently write out the three cost/benefit formulas from memory and apply them to the inoculation example from the chapter, explaining the private and external benefit

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: if private costs equal social costs for an action, what does this tell you about whether an externality exists?

Homework.text: Explain, using the car journey example, why private costs and social costs are not always equal

LO.text: Students will be able to explain and diagrammatically show negative production externalities and the resulting deadweight welfare loss

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains negative production externalities using the toxic waste and plastic waste examples, then demonstrates Figure 33.5 (MEC, MSC, MPC curves, socially optimum output Q vs actual output Q1, deadweight welfare loss triangle xyz)
We do: Class labels a copy of Figure 33.5 together, identifying the socially optimum output, the actual output and the deadweight welfare loss triangle
You do: Students independently sketch their own negative production externality diagram for a different real-world example (e.g. a factory emitting smoke) and label the deadweight welfare loss

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: why does a negative production externality result in overproduction relative to the socially optimum level?

Homework.text: Explain why the triangular area xyz in Figure 33.5 is called the 'deadweight welfare loss'

LO.text: Students will be able to explain and diagrammatically show positive production externalities and negative consumption externalities

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains positive production externalities using the vaccine and tree-planting examples (Figure 33.6, underproduction) and negative consumption externalities using the passive smoking and sports stadium examples (Figure 33.7, overconsumption)
We do: Class compares Figures 33.6 and 33.7 together, agreeing as a group on why one results in underproduction and the other in overconsumption relative to the social optimum
You do: Students independently explain, in writing, why passive smoking results in a marginal social benefit curve below the marginal private benefit curve

Consolidation.text: Traffic light self-assessment: can students explain the difference between a production externality and a consumption externality?

Homework.text: Choose one real-world example of a positive production externality and one of a negative consumption externality, and explain the third party affected in each

LO.text: Students will be able to explain and diagrammatically show positive consumption externalities

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains positive consumption externalities using the education and free healthcare examples (Figure 33.8, MSB above MPB, underconsumption)
We do: Class begins Activity 33.2 together as a group discussion, identifying local examples of each of the four types of externality near their school or college
You do: Students independently complete Activity 33.2 — producing a poster showing the four types of externality with diagrams and gathered evidence

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: why is a positive consumption externality a key argument for government provision of merit goods like education?

Homework.text: Explain why free healthcare is said to produce a marginal external benefit, referencing who benefits beyond the individual receiving treatment

LO.text: Students will be able to explain asymmetric information and distinguish between adverse selection and moral hazard

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains asymmetric information using the used car/scooter market example (Figure 33.9), then distinguishes hidden characteristics/adverse selection from hidden actions/moral hazard using the insurance and bank loan examples
We do: Class discusses, as a group, why good quality used cars get driven out of the market when buyers cannot tell good cars from bad ones
You do: Students independently complete Activity 33.3 — researching the market for used cars or scooters in their own country and identifying evidence of asymmetric information

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: give one example of adverse selection and one example of moral hazard, explaining the difference between them

Homework.text: Explain, using the healthcare example, why doctors and patients are said to have asymmetric information

LO.text: Students will be able to explain the stages of a cost-benefit analysis and apply Chapter 33 concepts to exam-style questions

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains the four stages of cost-benefit analysis (Figure 33.10) using the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor case study
We do: Class works through exam-style multiple choice Questions 1-3 together, agreeing on the correct answer and reasoning as a group
You do: Students independently attempt exam-style multiple choice Questions 4-7 under timed conditions, then peer-mark

Consolidation.text: Whole-class review of the multiple choice answers, with students justifying their reasoning for Q5 (which project is most likely to be funded) and Q6 (deadweight welfare loss)

Homework.text: Complete the chapter's self-evaluation checklist, rating yourself against each learning intention, and note one topic from this chapter you still need to revise

LO.text: Students will be able to describe the WiFi (CSMA/CA), Bluetooth and WiMax wireless protocols

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains CSMA/CA and distributed control function (DCF) for WiFi, then briefly explains Bluetooth (IEEE 802.15) and WiMax (IEEE 802.16) and their typical uses
We do: Class discusses, as a group, what happens under CSMA/CA when a WiFi device does not receive an acknowledgement after transmitting
You do: Students independently write a short comparison of WiFi, Bluetooth and WiMax, focusing on typical range and use case for each

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: why must CSMA/CA wait for a random time interval after a suspected collision rather than retrying immediately?

Homework.text: Research the typical range and data rate of Bluetooth and explain why it is unsuitable for connecting an entire office network

LO.text: Students will be able to describe how the BitTorrent protocol allows peer-to-peer file sharing

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains the BitTorrent protocol using the torrent/tracker/swarm/piece terminology and Figure 14.6, demonstrating the roles of seeds, leeches and lurkers
We do: Class calculates the share ratio for a given peer together (uploaded/downloaded data), deciding whether that peer has a positive or negative impact on the swarm
You do: Students independently complete Activity 14A Q3 — explaining the terms peer, swarm, tracker, leech and seed, and how peers acting as leeches could be dealt with

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: what is the difference between a leech and a lurker in a BitTorrent swarm?

Homework.text: Explain why having more seeds in a swarm speeds up the file downloading process for other peers

LO.text: Students will be able to explain circuit switching and evaluate its advantages and disadvantages

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains the three stages of circuit switching (establish, transfer, terminate) and demonstrates the dedicated route example using Figure 14.7, then reviews the pros/cons in Table 14.3
We do: Class traces the dedicated route from 'A' to 'B' in Figure 14.7 together (A-R2, R2-R5, R5-R8, R8-R7, R7-R10, R10-B), confirming why all packets must follow this single route
You do: Students independently list three real-world uses of circuit switching and explain why a dedicated channel suits each use

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: why does circuit switching work better than packet switching for real-time applications?

Homework.text: Explain, in your own words, one advantage and one disadvantage of circuit switching not yet discussed in class

LO.text: Students will be able to explain packet switching and compare it with circuit switching

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains packet switching using Figure 14.8 (each packet takes its own path, reassembly needed), then compares circuit and packet switching using Table 14.5
We do: Class works through Example 14.1 together — explaining the poor performance of video conferencing over packet switching and what features of circuit switching would improve it
You do: Students independently write out the pros/cons comparison from Table 14.4 in their own words, listing two advantages and two disadvantages of packet switching

Consolidation.text: Traffic light self-assessment: can students complete Table 14.5's comparison of circuit and packet switching from memory?

Homework.text: Explain why packet switching charges users only for the duration of connectivity, while circuit switching charges based on distance and duration

LO.text: Students will be able to explain how hop numbers and checksums prevent problems in packet switching
Students will be able to describe the contents of a packet header

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains hopping (preventing lost packets clogging the network) and checksums (error checking), then demonstrates the packet header structure using Figure 14.9 and the detailed bit breakdown
We do: Class works through Example 14.2 together, describing how packet switching is used to download a web page, step by step
You do: Students independently complete Activity 14A Q4a — describing the difference between a packet header and a routing table

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: what happens to a packet if its hop number reaches zero before it reaches its destination?

Homework.text: Explain what a checksum is used for in a packet header, and what happens if the checksum does not match at the destination

LO.text: Students will be able to explain how routing tables are used to forward packets to their destination

Activities.text: I do: Teacher explains routing tables using Figure 14.10, demonstrating how a packet header is compared against the routing table to determine the next hop
We do: Class works through Activity 14A Q4b together, explaining how the packet header and routing table work together to route a package
You do: Students independently complete Activity 14A Q5 — explaining how packet switching could be used for a VoIP video call and describing any problems that might occur

Consolidation.text: Cold-call Q&A: name three pieces of information stored in a routing table

Homework.text: Explain what happens at a router if no route can be found for a packet, or if its hop number reaches zero

LO.text: Students will be able to apply Chapter 14 concepts to exam-style questions covering protocols, circuit switching and packet switching

Activities.text: I do: Teacher reviews the chapter's key concepts (TCP/IP layers, email protocols, BitTorrent, circuit vs packet switching) using the End of chapter questions as a framework
We do: Class works through End of chapter Question 1 (matching peer-to-peer terms, completing the TCP/IP diagram) together, agreeing on answers as a group
You do: Students independently attempt End of chapter Questions 3 and 4 under timed conditions, covering circuit switching, packet switching and routing
