LO.text: Understand how text is represented in a computer system using character sets, and compare ASCII and Extended ASCII in terms of character representation and storage requirements.

Activities.text: I do: Direct instruction demonstrating how characters are represented as binary values in computer memory using character sets, detailing how 7-bit standard ASCII maps 128 characters (2^7) and requires 1 byte per character (with a leading zero)

We do: Worked example on the board converting short words (e.g. 'CAB' or 'Cat') into binary and hexadecimal representation using an ASCII lookup table, discussing why Extended ASCII (8-bit) was developed to support 256 characters
You do: Complete Textbook Activity 1.2.1, converting given text strings into binary and hex representations and calculating the total memory required in bytes

Consolidation.text: Exit ticket: ask students to write down the main limitation of standard ASCII when representing international text and how Extended ASCII partially addresses this

Homework.text: Calculate the file size in bytes and bits for a 500-word plain text document stored using standard ASCII, showing all working

LO.text: Explain the purpose and structure of Unicode as a character set, comparing its advantages and disadvantages over ASCII for global character representation.

Activities.text: I do: Teacher-led explanation of Unicode, focusing on UTF-8 and UTF-16 bit formats, demonstrating how expanding to 16-bit or 32-bit enables representation of over 100,000 unique symbols, including non-Latin alphabets and emojis
We do: Compare ASCII and Unicode side-by-side on the board in terms of character coverage, bit-depth per character, and file storage impact; analyse a comparative scenario question together
You do: Complete textbook practice questions requiring students to compare ASCII and Unicode, detailing specific trade-offs between storage capacity and multilingual representation

Consolidation.text: Think-pair-share: why was Unicode designed to be backward-compatible with standard ASCII, and what impact does this have on software engineering?

Homework.text: Write a concise comparison paragraph (150 words) detailing why a global web platform would choose Unicode over ASCII

LO.text: Describe how sound is converted from analogue to digital format, and analyse how sampling rate and sample resolution affect sound quality and file size.

Activities.text: I do: Demonstrate sound digitisation using dynamic diagrams of analogue sound waves, explaining the roles of Analogue-to-Digital Converters (ADC), sampling rate (Hz), and sample resolution (bits per sample)
We do: Step-by-step calculation on the board to find the file size of an uncompressed audio recording (File Size = Sampling Rate x Sample Resolution x Time in seconds x Channels)
You do: Solve Textbook Activity 1.2.2 calculations on audio file sizing and evaluate the trade-offs in quality vs. file size when increasing sampling rates

Consolidation.text: Whiteboard quick check: calculate the file size in kilobits for a 10-second mono audio clip sampled at 44.1 kHz with a 16-bit resolution

Homework.text: Complete textbook end-of-section practice questions on sound representation and sampling trade-offs

LO.text: Explain how bitmap images are stored using pixels, colour depth, and resolution, and calculate the file size of bitmap images.

Activities.text: I do: Model how bitmap graphics are constructed using a pixel grid, explaining resolution (dimensions in pixels) and colour depth (2^n colours for n bits per pixel)
We do: Guided calculation of bitmap file size (File Size = Width x Height x Colour Depth) in bits and bytes, working through a 24-bit TrueColor image example
You do: Complete Textbook Activity 1.2.3, calculating file sizes for various bitmap resolutions and colour depths, and determining how reducing colour depth alters image fidelity

Consolidation.text: 3-2-1 summary: 3 factors affecting bitmap size, 2 colour depth examples, 1 key difference between vector and bitmap concepts

Homework.text: Calculate the storage required for a 1920 x 1080 pixel image at 24-bit colour depth, converting the final answer into Megabytes (MB)
